title: Essential Greetings
description: Start friendly conversations with everyday polite greetings.

words.fact: The most common polite greeting in Korea. Give a gentle nod or bow as you say it!
Use this to show gratitude to teachers, parents, shopkeepers, and friends.
A clear, polite way to agree. Saying it with a smile always sounds pleasant.
A polite way to decline or disagree without sounding harsh.
Say this when enjoying a tasty meal or snack—cooks love hearing it!
Say this to someone who is leaving when you are staying.

title: Numbers 1 to 6
description: Master basic Sino-Korean counting words for prices, dates, and order.

words.fact: Also sounds like the Korean word for 'work' and 'day'!
Short and sweet! Also the word for 'teeth' in Korean.

title: Family & People
description: Learn how to talk about family members and people around you.

words.fact: An affectionate, warm word that children and adults often use for their mother.
The everyday friendly title for dad in Korean homes.
Traditionally refers to peers of the same age, but widely used for close buddies!
'-nim' is an honorific suffix showing deep respect for mentors and teachers.
Can mean younger brother ('nam-dongsaeng') or younger sister ('yeo-dongsaeng').
Literally connects to the characters for 'household' and 'tribe'!

title: Vibrant Colors
description: Name bright and vivid colors you see every day.

words.fact: 'Saek' means color. You see lots of red in Korean chili paste (gochujang)!
The color of clear skies and the East Sea in Korea.
Often associated with sweet yellow Forsythia flowers (Gaenari) blooming in spring.
The fresh color of pine trees, jade, and summer mountains.
Historically, Koreans were known as the 'white-clad folk' for wearing clean white Hanbok.
Sleek and classic, like ink used in traditional East Asian calligraphy.

title: Delicious Foods
description: Common Korean meal staples and tasty food terms.

words.fact: 'Bap meogeosseoyo?' (Have you eaten rice?) is a warm everyday way to ask 'How are you?'
A super handy word in restaurants: 'Mul juseyo' means 'Please give me water'!
Korea's famous fermented vegetable dish made with Napa cabbage, radish, and seasonings.
Key ingredient in Korean BBQ favorites like bulgogi and galbi!
Fun fact: 'Sagwa' means both crisp apple and sincere apology in Korean!
Korean banana milk ('banana-mat uyu') in the chubby bottle is a beloved classic snack.

title: Friendly Animals
description: Favorite pets and wild creatures in Korean.

words.fact: An affectionate word for a puppy or pet dog. Korean dogs bark 'meong-meong'!
Korean cats meow 'ya-ong'! Street cats are lovingly called 'gil-goyangi'.
In Korean folklore, a moon rabbit pounds sweet rice cakes on the full moon!
Bears play a starring role in the ancient Korean foundation myth of Dangun.
Short one-syllable word. Magpies ('kkachi') are considered lucky birds in Korea.

title: School & Stationery
description: Words for school life, writing tools, and study time.

words.fact: Elementary school in Korea is called 'chodeung-hakgyo'.
Reading a book is 'chaek-eul ilgeo-yo'.
A handy tool for practicing Hangul stroke orders!
Borrowed from Portuguese 'capa' / Japanese centuries ago into modern Korean.
Literally combines 'chaek' (book) and 'sang' (table)!
Helps everyone stay punctual for morning classes.

title: Feelings & Moods
description: Express how your day is going and share your emotions.

words.fact: From the noun 'haengbok' (happiness) plus polite 'haeyo' (doing/feeling).
Used constantly in Korea to say 'Sounds great!' or 'I like that idea!'
Expresses sadness or empathy when watching an emotional story.
Great phrase after a long day of sports, studying, or travel.
Say this when you're looking forward to an amusement park or party!
One of the most reassuring everyday phrases in the Korean language.

title: Body & Senses
description: Basic body parts to describe yourself and stay healthy.

words.fact: 'Nun' means both 'eye' and 'falling snow'—you tell them apart by context!
A punchy single syllable that's super easy to remember.
Used for speaking and tasting delicious Korean dishes!

title: Daily Action Verbs
description: Everyday action words in polite conversational form.

words.fact: From the verb 'gada' (to go). 'Haggyo-e gayo' = I'm going to school!
'Eoseo wayo' means welcome, please come in!
From 'meokda' (to eat). 'Masitge meogeoyo' = Enjoy your meal!
Used when drinking water, juice, or warm tea.
'Jal jayo' is the sweet, polite phrase for 'Sleep well' / 'Good night'!
From 'gongbu' (study) + 'haeyo' (doing). You are doing it right now with Korean!
